note: You are reading the item catalogue of a game — the held objects the player picks up and carries, each with a display name and 'examine' text (what the player reads on a close look), plus, for each item, where it is used in the game (a hotspot that hands it over, an effect that spends it, a gate that requires it). Judge only what is on the page; you have no knowledge of the author's intent beyond what the entries and their uses show. An item's examine text should describe what the thing IS and DOES — material, condition, function — and never what it means (no memory, symbolism, or sentiment); grade concrete usefulness, not poetry. The top level is a catalogue a person would ship, not a flawless one. For each criterion, pick the single level (0-4) whose description best matches, and quote specific item names and examine lines as evidence.

criteria.name: examine_substance
criteria._authoring: The placeholder test. The persistent failure is an examine string that restates the name or is a bare stub ('a key', 'an item', 'a useful object', empty), so looking rewards the player with nothing. Mechanically an item only needs a name to exist, so a stub examine is the default attractor. NOT gated — a mid examine is forgivable (a broken name is worse; the gate lives on item_naming). Keep the 'never what it means' register: an examine that drifts into symbolism/memory is not top-level even if vivid.
criteria.description: Does each item's examine text reward a close look — stating concretely what the object is and does (material, condition, function) rather than restating the name or offering a stub?

levels.0: Placeholder. Examine text is a bare stub or a restatement of the name — 'a key', 'an item', 'a useful object', or blank — telling the player nothing the name didn't already. Looking is unrewarded.
levels.1: Barely there. A short generic gloss adds one vague adjective ('an old key', 'a rusty tool') but no specific material, condition, or function; the player learns almost nothing by examining.
levels.2: Functional. The examine plainly states what the object is and roughly what it does — enough to know why you'd carry it — but stays generic, reading the same as any game's key or rope or note.
levels.3: Specific. The examine gives concrete, in-world detail — material, condition, or how it works — that ties the object to this game and rewards the look, describing the thing itself and not what it symbolizes.
levels.4: Vivid and exact. Grounded, functional detail makes the object feel real and hints at its use, with no line of meaning, memory, or symbolism; examining it is its own small payoff.

criteria.name: item_naming
criteria._authoring: Load-bearing here — a broken or confusing name reads as unfinished, so it's gated. CLARITY is the axis, NOT invention: a clear familiar name ('Vibranium Sword') is fully shippable and must NOT score below a coined one; an invented name that costs readability ('Vibranium Shallot' for a sword) is WORSE, not better. In-world flavor is a bonus stacked on a clear name, never a substitute for it. GATE: below level 2 (a generic token / raw id, or a coined name a player can't parse) caps the overall — a catalogue of 'Item'/'key_1' or opaque names looks unfinished. Familiar-but-clear sits at level 2, the shippable bar.
criteria.description: Does each item's name clearly and cleanly identify the object — a plain, readable name a player instantly understands — with in-world flavor as a bonus that never costs clarity?

levels.0: Broken. Names are bare category words — 'Item', 'Object', 'Thing' — or the raw snake_case id echoed as a name ('brass_key'); the player can't tell what they hold.
levels.1: Unclear. Either a vague category-plus-filler that still doesn't say what the object is, or a coined/invented name a player can't parse at a glance (an in-world word standing alone with no familiar anchor) — the name costs more clarity than it adds.
levels.2: Clear and shippable. Each name plainly and correctly identifies the object; a player instantly knows what it is — 'Brass Key', 'Rope', 'Vibranium Sword'. Familiar is fine here — clarity is the bar, and a generic-but-clear name meets it.
levels.3: Clear with flavor. Names read instantly AND carry a touch of this game's world — a familiar object anchored with apt in-world specificity ('Cellar Key', 'Harbor-master's Ledger') — without ever sacrificing readability.
levels.4: Clear, specific, characterful. Every name is instantly readable and specific to this game, the wording itself doing a little characterizing work, with zero loss of clarity and no reaching for exotic effect.

criteria.name: items_matter
criteria._authoring: The earns-its-place test. The build is demand-driven — an item exists only because something references it — so 'every item is used at least once' is guaranteed by construction and lands at level 2, not the top. Level 0 anchors a decorative or duplicated catalogue; the top requires items that interlock (combine, chain, gate a path) so the list is exactly what the game needs.
criteria.description: Does every item earn its place — obtained and spent in a real interaction (a gate it opens, a step in a chain) — with no decorative or redundant entries?

levels.0: Decorative catalogue. Items carry no real use — nothing meaningfully takes, spends, or gates on them, or entries duplicate each other; the list is padding.
levels.1: Mostly inert. A few items do work but several are dead weight — picked up and never needed, or gating nothing.
levels.2: Each used once. Every item is referenced by some take, use, or gate, but the uses are shallow — a straight fetch-and-hand-over with no consequence if it were skipped.
levels.3: Earns its place. Every item is obtained and then spent in a real interaction — a gate it opens, a step in a chain — and removing any one would break a puzzle or block a path.
levels.4: Load-bearing and interlocked. Every item drives a specific gate or chain, several combine or feed later steps, and the catalogue is exactly what the game needs — nothing decorative, nothing missing.
